content.title: Glossary | Practical Law
content.text: A compensatory award that represents a company's unsecured and unfunded promise to deliver a specified number of shares of common stock (or cash equal to the value of the shares of common stock) to an employee or other service provider in the future if certain performance vesting criteria are met. Like performance shares, PSUs are subject to forfeiture until they vest.While PSUs are similar to restricted stock units (RSUs), vesting for PSUs typically includes both performance requirements and continuous service requirements. Performance is measured over a specified period, called the performance period (often three years). While the award is expressed as a "target" number of PSUs, the number of PSUs actually earned depends on performance over the performance period (often it is possible to earn between 0% and 200% of the target number of PSUs).Holders of PSUs do not have voting or other shareholder rights because they are not the beneficial owner of the underlying shares, but some companies grant dividend equivalents in connection with PSUs.PSUs are not subject to tax at grant. At vesting, the fair market value (FMV) of the PSUs is subject to tax under the Federal Insurance Contributions Act (FICA) and Federal Unemployment Tax Act (FUTA). For federal income tax purposes, the grantee recognizes ordinary income on the FMV of the PSUs when they are settled, and the employer is entitled to a corresponding tax deduction. If settled in shares, when the shares are sold, any gain or loss is taxable as short-term or long-term capital gain or loss, depending on how long the shares are held. PSUs are preferred by shareholders because of the strong link they create between pay and performance. © 2026 Thomson Reuters. All rights reserved.
